label: Colonic_Adenocarcinoma_Arising_In_Adenoma
answer_markdown:
## Key Facts

- Colonic adenocarcinoma arising in adenoma ("malignant polyp") is defined by invasion through the muscularis mucosa into submucosa (pT1)[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].
- "Intramucosal carcinoma" (limited to lamina propria/muscularis mucosa) is not considered invasive in the colon and is staged as pTis, biologically equivalent to high-grade dysplasia[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].
- Desmoplastic stromal reaction is the key histologic hallmark distinguishing true invasion from pseudoinvasion.
- Key benign mimics: pseudoinvasion (misplaced glands with lamina propria/hemosiderin), colitis cystica profunda, prolapse-type changes.
- Immunohistochemistry (CK20, CDX2, SATB2) is useful for ambiguous cases or to rule out metastasis, but not required for classic cases[Pathoutlines].
- Prognosis and management depend on margin status and high-risk histologic features: lymphovascular invasion, poor differentiation, and high tumor budding[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].

## Terminology

- Malignant polyp, adenoma with invasive carcinoma, or adenocarcinoma arising in adenoma: neoplasm with submucosal invasion through muscularis mucosa[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].
- "Intramucosal carcinoma": invasion confined to lamina propria/within muscularis mucosa only; pTis in colon, not considered truly invasive and managed as high-grade dysplasia[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].
- "Adenoma-like adenocarcinoma" preferred over "villous adenocarcinoma" for well-differentiated tumor imitating villous adenoma[Pathoutlines].
- Distinction between pTis (intramucosal, biologically non-invasive in colon) and pT1 (submucosal invasion, true carcinoma) is critical for prognosis/treatment.

## Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria

- **Essential:**
  - Invasive adenocarcinoma arising in pre-existing adenoma (tubular, tubulovillous, or villous)[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].
    - Invasion through muscularis mucosa into submucosa (pT1)[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].
    - Desmoplastic stroma surrounding irregular or angulated malignant glands at invasive edge.
    - Cytologic features: increased nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, loss of polarity.
    - Clear distinction from pseudoinvasion: pseudoinvasion shows glands surrounded by lamina propria and often hemosiderin, lacking desmoplasia.
    - Use of Haggitt (pedunculated) and Kikuchi/Kudo SM1–SM3 (sessile) levels to grade depth of invasion.
- **Desirable:**
  - Document high-risk features: lymphovascular/perineural invasion, poor differentiation, high tumor budding[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].
  - Margin status: measure and report distance to excision margin.
  - Ancillary IHC (CK20, CDX2, SATB2) for origin, especially in ambiguous or non-classic presentations.
  - Correlate with polyp type and clinical context.

## Etiology/Pathogenesis

- Adenoma–carcinoma sequence: sequential mutations in APC, KRAS, TP53[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenoma.html), [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).
- Pathways:
  - Chromosomal instability (~70–80%) most common[Pathoutlines].
  - Microsatellite instability (MMR defects) observed in a subset, especially certain histologic variants[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).
- Increased risk in hereditary syndromes (FAP, Lynch syndrome); Western diet and sedentary lifestyle are epidemiologic factors[Pathoutlines].

## Clinical Issues

- Often detected incidentally on screening; incidence increases with age[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].
- May occur anywhere in colon (more common left-sided but possible throughout).
- Typical symptoms if present: anemia (right), change in bowel habits (left), bleeding.
- Progression of adenoma to carcinoma over 10–15 years.
- Treatment: local polypectomy for low-risk; surgical resection for high-risk features (deep invasion, LVI, poor differentiation, positive/close margin).

## Staging

- **pTis:** Intramucosal carcinoma—confined to lamina propria/muscularis mucosa. Biologically equivalent to high-grade dysplasia; no risk for nodal/distant metastasis in colon.
- **pT1:** Invasion through muscularis mucosa into submucosa (defines invasive carcinoma).
  - Haggitt levels (1–4) for pedunculated polyps; Kikuchi/Kudo Sm1–Sm3 for sessile lesions[Textbooks].
- Lymph node and margin status essential for further staging.

## Macroscopic

- Polypoid lesion, variable morphology: pedunculated, sessile, or flat.
- Tumor may be tan-red, firm, possibly ulcerated.
- Villous/tubulovillous adenomas more likely to harbor invasion[Textbooks].
- Invasive foci may produce induration or thickening at base.

## Microscopic

- Transition from adenomatous (dysplastic) to overtly malignant (invasive) glands, crossing muscularis mucosa into submucosa.
- Invasive component: desmoplastic (fibrotic) response, cribriform or complex glands, marked cytologic atypia, increased mitoses, loss of polarity.
- Tumor budding: small discohesive clusters (<5 cells) seen at invasive front.
- Lymphovascular invasion and necrosis may be present.
- Morphologic grading:
  - Well differentiated: 15–20% (mostly gland-forming)[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).
  - Moderately differentiated: 60–70% (intermediate gland formation, more atypia).
  - Poorly differentiated: 15–20% (less than 50% glandular, sheets of cells, marked atypia, often right-sided)[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).
- **Pseudoinvasion:** Displaced glands in submucosa, surrounded by lamina propria and hemosiderin, with rounded borders and no desmoplasia.
- Mucinous and signet-ring components may occur in adenocarcinoma arising in adenoma.

![Malignant polyp: Invasive adenocarcinoma arising in tubular adenoma](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/colontumorcarcinomaarisingJoldoshova03.jpg)
![Desmoplastic stroma with tumor budding at invasion front](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/colontumorcarcinomaarisingJoldoshova09.jpg)
![Lymphovascular invasion highlighted](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/imgau/colontumorcarcinomaarisingJoldoshova08.jpg)

## Ancillary Tests

- **Immunohistochemistry:**
  - CK20: positive in most colonic adenocarcinomas, aids in diagnosis[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).
  - CDX2: highly sensitive and specific for colorectal origin; loss suggests high-grade tumor[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).
  - SATB2: positive in colorectal carcinoma[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).
  - CK7: usually negative, but may be co-expressed in rectal adenocarcinomas or non-colorectal primaries[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).
- **Molecular:**
  - APC, KRAS, TP53 frequently mutated[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).
  - Screen for microsatellite instability with MMR panel (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2).
- **Diagnostic utility:** IHC not required in classic cases, but critical for distinguishing colorectal primary from metastasis (especially in CK7/CK20/CDX2 profile).

## Differential Diagnosis

| Feature                         | Adenocarcinoma Arising in Adenoma        | Adenoma with Pseudoinvasion                | Colitis Cystica Profunda             | Endometrioid Adenocarcinoma (Endometriosis)     |
|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| Desmoplastic (fibrotic) stroma   | Present at invasive front                | Absent; glands show lamina propria/hemosiderin | Not present; abundant mucin lakes   | +/-; may have stromal reaction if invasive      |
| Cytologic atypia                 | Marked, loss of polarity, pleomorphism   | Low to moderate, similar to adenoma        | Absent (benign glands)               | Variable: typically moderate to marked          |
| Lymphovascular invasion          | May be present                           | Absent                                     | Absent                               | Can be present                                 |
| Tumor budding                    | Present at invasion edge                 | Absent                                     | Absent                               | Variable                                       |
| Misplaced/submucosal glands      | Angulated, irregular, with desmoplasia   | Rounded, encased in lamina propria, hemosiderin, no desmoplasia | Benign crypts, cystically dilated   | Endometrioid glands in background of endometriosis|
| Clinical context                 | Usually within polyp, may or may not be symptomatic | Pedunculated polyp, usually asymptomatic   | Associated with mucosal prolapse or trauma | Site of endometriosis, often women             |
| Staining profile                 | CK20+, CDX2+, SATB2+, CK7–               | Same as adenoma                            | Consistent with benign mucosa        | CK7+, PAX8+, often ER/PR+ (not CDX2+)          |
| Clinical significance            | Malignant, requires full staging         | Benign mimic                               | Benign mimic                         | Malignant, distinct from colonic carcinoma      |

- **Adenoma with pseudoinvasion:** Bland glands in submucosa surrounded by lamina propria/hemosiderin, rounded, no desmoplasia or high-grade atypia[Pathoutlines, Textbooks].
- **Colitis cystica profunda:** Cystically dilated, benign crypts deep to muscularis mucosa, in pools of mucin, no atypia; often related to mucosal prolapse[Pathoutlines].
- **Mucosal prolapse syndrome, localized polypoid colitis, and repair:** Benign processes with architectural/cellular changes simulating neoplasia, but no cytologic grade or desmoplasia[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)].
- **Endometrioid adenocarcinoma (endometriosis):** Endometrioid glands in colon wall, variable atypia, PAX8/ER/PR+, CDX2-/CK20-; consider in lesions with endometriotic stroma or history of endometriosis[Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumoradenocarcinoma.html).

## Prognostic Factors

- High-risk features:
  - Poor differentiation
  - Lymphovascular invasion
  - High-grade tumor budding
  - Positive or close (<1 mm) excision margin
  - Deep submucosal invasion (Haggitt 4, Sm3)[Textbooks, [Pathoutlines](https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/colontumorcarcinomaarising.html)]
- Favorable outcome expected when none of above present and excised with negative margin; surgery required if any high-risk feature present.

## Illustrative Cases

- Case: Pedunculated tubular adenoma with foci of invasive adenocarcinoma, desmoplasia, lymphovascular space invasion, and high tumor budding at invasive front[Pathoutlines, Textbooks].

cards.excerpt: Entity: Non-ampullary adenoma Section: microscopic organs, presumably associated with gastric heterotopia, and therefore the general term PGA is preferred. Their mutation profile, in both stomach and duodenum, exhibits a notable frequency of GNAS mutations, making them molecularly linked and distinct from other precursor lesions. Immunohistochemically, PGAs show MUC6 expression (usually extensive) and a variable extent of MUC5AC expression. Serrated lesions and polyps, similar to their colonic counterparts (see section Colorectal serrated lesions and polyps, are identifiable in the small intestine, frequently associated with dysplasia or adenocarcinoma.

cards.title: Adenocarcinoma — Exophytic lesion
cards.excerpt:
Microscopic (histologic) description
Usually well or moderately differentiated gland forming carcinoma with marked desmoplasia, particularly at edge of tumor
Glands often cribriform and filled with necrotic debris (dirty necrosis), in both primary and metastatic sites
Inflammatory cells and scattered neuroendocrine cells are common (Pol J Pathol 2005;56:89)
Intramural venous invasion may be easier to identify using an elastin stain (J Clin Pathol 2002;55:17)

cards.title: Adenocarcinoma — Pathophysiology
cards.excerpt:
Cases deemed mucosal anal adenocarcinomas may arise from transitional mucosa between anus and rectum or may actually arise in the rectum and spread downward (JCO Oncol Pract 2020;16:635)
Extramucosal cases may arise from anal glands, from congenital anorectal duplications or along a fistula tract (Dis Colon Rectum 1998;41:992)
Rare, mucosa based cases are linked to high risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection (Mod Pathol 2020;33:944, Int J Surg Pathol 2021;29:672, Br J Cancer 2018;118:1302)

cards.title: Adenocarcinoma — Etiology
cards.excerpt:
Proposed etiologic associations include chronic fistula, anal Crohn's disease and anal sexual intercourse (Semin Surg Oncol 1994;10:235)
Though rare, chronic fistulas in patients with Crohn's disease can become malignant, potentially due to long term injury and repair of the intestinal tract or prolonged immunosuppression (J Gastrointest Surg 2010;14:66)

cards.title: Adenocarcinoma — Mucosal anal adenocarcinoma
cards.excerpt:
Extramucosal anal adenocarcinomaMicroscopic (histologic) description
4 subtypes have been described based on tumor origin
Mucosal anal adenocarcinomas arise from the mucosal surface and have an intestinal appearance mimicking rectal adenocarcinoma (e.g., pencillate nuclei, amphophilic cytoplasm, cribriforming, some degree of mucin)
Some of these are perhaps of rectal origin but may be deemed anal adenocarcinomas clinically
Extramucosal anal gland adenocarcinomas form haphazardly dispersed small glands with scant mucin production that invade the wall of the anorectal area without an intraluminal component; overlying epithelium may be intact or secondarily involved (Cancer 2001;92:2045)

cards.title: Adenocarcinoma — Some cases may demonstrate abundant mucin or signet ring cells
cards.excerpt:
Extramucosal fistula associated adenocarcinomas are often mucinous (> 50% of tumor volume consists of mucin) and generally have an intestinal appearance otherwise
Extramucosal non-anal gland non-fistula associated adenocarcinomas can vary histologically but often have a somewhat intestinal appearance without involving the mucosal surface
HPV related cases show papillary or villiform structures lined by columnar cells that often contain abundant mucin (Mod Pathol 2020;33:944)
Single neoplastic cells may colonize the overlying and adjacent squamous mucosa (extramammary Paget disease) (Int J Surg Pathol 2021;29:672)

cards.title: Adenoma with invasive carcinoma — Essential features
cards.excerpt:
Colorectal adenoma with invasive carcinoma represents the earliest form of carcinoma because submucosal invasion leads to further risk for lymphatic and vascular metastasis even if the polyp / tumor has been completely resected (Gastroenterology 2004;127:385)
Colorectal adenomas with intramucosal carcinomas limited to the surface epithelium, lamina propria or muscularis mucosae are staged as carcinoma in situ (Tis) and should be excluded from this category (Am J Gastroenterol 2020;115:1751)
On a limited biopsy specimen when a clinical mass lesion is identified, we can diagnose invasive carcinoma in a colorectal adenoma if we see marked desmoplasia, infiltrative pattern, poorly differentiated morphology or lymphovascular space invasion (LVI) (Gastroenterology 1995;108:1657)

cards.title: Adenoma with invasive carcinoma — Epidemiology
cards.excerpt:
Prevalence of malignant polyps is between 0.2% and 12.0% (average: ~5.0%) in endoscopic polypectomies (Endoscopy 1995;27:153)
Incidence is increasing due to more efficacious colonoscopy screening programs, which are fundamental in the prevention of colorectal cancer and the treatment of some advanced polyps (World J Gastroenterol 2010;16:3103)
Malignant polyps are also classified based on the depth of invasion, which is the most important feature; in 1985, Haggitt et al. put forward a classification system for pedunculated and sessile polyps based on the depth of invasion of adenocarcinoma (Gastroenterology 1985;89:328)

cards.title: Adenoma with invasive carcinoma — Pathophysiology
cards.excerpt:
95% of colorectal cancers arise from adenomatous polyps and follow adenoma - carcinoma sequence, which is an indolent process taking many years to progress after a stepwise collection of genetic alterations
Sessile serrated adenoma is presumed to be the precursor of right sided adenocarcinomas with high levels of microsatellite instability (MSI-H) (Am J Gastroenterol 2012;107:1315)

cards.title: Adenoma with invasive carcinoma — Lymphatic / venous vessel involvement
cards.excerpt:
Histologic factors that have adverse prognostic factors for distant metastasis are as follows (Mod Pathol 2017;30:1299)
Quantity of tumor budding (Hum Pathol 2016;47:4)
Depth or area of submucosal invasion (submucosal invasion > 1 mm) (World J Surg 2018;42:2635)
In en block resections of pedunculated or nonpedunculated colorectal lesions with submucosal invasion, the pathologists need to measure and report the depth of invasion, distance of the tumor from the deep and lateral surgical resection margins, in addition to prognostic histologic features, such as degree of differentiation, presence or absence of lymphovascular invasion and tumor budding

cards.title: Adenoma with invasive carcinoma — Treatment
cards.excerpt:
Polypectomy with complete removal of the malignant colorectal polyp; prevention of colorectal cancer progression is the primary goal
Endoscopic resection can provide complete resection and obviate the higher morbidity, mortality and cost associated with alternative surgical treatment
Complete excision with conventional endoscopic snare polypectomy for < 1 cm adenomas, which accounts for 80 - 90% of colorectal polyps (Am J Surg Pathol 2018;42:1083)
Cold or hot snare polypectomy (with or without submucosal injection) to remove 10 - 19 mm nonpedunculated lesions
Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) are used for > 20 mm nonpedunculated colorectal polyps but are usually only available in specialized centers
Benefit of EMR and ESD is the ability to obtain 1 large piece of tissue, avoiding fragmented excision with clear margins and making it easier to orient, section and evaluate margins
Colectomy with lymph node dissection is recommended for pedunculated polyps with any unfavorable histology, invasion into submucosa of bowel wall (Haggitt level 4) and any sessile / flat adenomas with invasion (Haggitt level 1 - 4)
First follow up surveillance colonoscopy is 6 months for larger colorectal polyps ≥ 20 mm and the interval to the next colonoscopy is at 1 year and then 3 years (Am J Surg Pathol 2018;42:1083)

cards.title: Adenoma with invasive carcinoma — Hemorrhage or hemosiderin deposition
cards.excerpt:
Sometimes acellular extracellular mucin associated with ruptured dilated mucinous cysts and inflammatory response may be noted; need to differentiate from an invasive mucinous carcinoma (colloid), which will have mucin pools with malignant cells, a feature lacking in pseudoinvasion
Colonic adenomatous polyps involving submucosal lymphoglandular complexes (Am J Surg Pathol 2018;42:1083):
Lymphoglandular complexes (LGCs) are lymphoid follicles, present in close apposition to lamina propria or muscularis mucosae or submucosa; rarely, colorectal adenomas involve submucosal lymphoglandular complexes, simulating invasive adenocarcinoma with associated extensive lymphoid response and presenting a diagnostic pitfall
Tumor is contained within the lymphoid tissue and lack infiltrating single cells / small clusters, poorly formed, fused and irregular glands, solid tumor nests, desmoplastic reaction and lymphovascular invasion

Sometimes acellular extracellular mucin associated with ruptured dilated mucinous cysts and inflammatory response may be noted; need to differentiate from an invasive mucinous carcinoma (colloid), which will have mucin pools with malignant cells, a feature lacking in pseudoinvasion
Colonic adenomatous polyps involving submucosal lymphoglandular complexes (Am J Surg Pathol 2018;42:1083):
Lymphoglandular complexes (LGCs) are lymphoid follicles, present in close apposition to lamina propria or muscularis mucosae or submucosa; rarely, colorectal adenomas involve submucosal lymphoglandular complexes, simulating invasive adenocarcinoma with associated extensive lymphoid response and presenting a diagnostic pitfall
Tumor is contained within the lymphoid tissue and lack infiltrating single cells / small clusters, poorly formed, fused and irregular glands, solid tumor nests, desmoplastic reaction and lymphovascular invasion

cards.title: Adenoma — Raised lesion at ampulla of VaterMicroscopic (histologic) description
cards.excerpt:
Tubular, tubulovillous or villous, similar to adenomas in colon, with approximately half tubular and half villous (Am J Clin Pathol 2009;132:506)
Low grade dysplasia demonstrates hyperchromatic, pencil shaped nuclei confined to the basal layer of cells, with limited architectural changes (Mod Pathol 2019;32:1291)
High grade dysplasia demonstrates large, rounded nuclei with loss of polarity, along with architectural abnormalities such as cribriforming (Mod Pathol 2019;32:1291)
Dysplastic epithelium may have only subtle changes of mild cellular stratification and fine chromatin pattern
Often contain prominent Paneth cells (with coarse, large, red-pink, refractile granules in supranuclear cytoplasm), endocrine cells (dark, red-purple, fine, small granules in basal cytoplasm) and goblet cells

missing_essentials: Table with details of distinguishing features of pseudoinvasion (including point that glands are often surrounded by lamina propria and hemosiderin, not desmoplasia, is only partly present and not fully clear as a table).

Statement that 'intramucosal carcinoma' is considered biologically equivalent to high-grade dysplasia and not considered invasive carcinoma in the colon—draft says this but reference to pTis definition could be clarified.
More explicit noting that for adenocarcinoma diagnosis, CK20, CDX2 and SATB2 can help especially in ambiguous cases, but not required.
Mimics such as mucosal prolapse syndrome, localized polypoid colitis, and repair are listed in evidence as benign processes that can simulate adenoma or carcinoma and could be more distinctly listed.
Some specific grading percentages: well (15-20%), moderate (60-70%), poor (15-20%), and their morphologic correlates, as per Pathology Outlines.
Diagnosis often does not require immunolabeling but may be important to distinguish metastatic tumors (e.g., CK7/20 profiles and reference to rare CK7+ cases in rectal tumors).
confusing: The table in Differential Diagnosis: The 'Location of misplaced glands' row does not fully clarify the difference between pseudoinvasion (submucosa, with lamina propria/hemosiderin, often in pedunculated polyps) vs. true invasive carcinoma, and colitis cystica profunda. Should clarify these more precisely.

In Essential and Desirable Diagnostic Criteria, 'intramucosal carcinoma' is stated under terminology, but the distinction with pTis and pT1 and the implications for treatment/prognosis should be made even more explicit per Pathology Outlines and textbooks.
entity_conflation: Features and management details for IBD-associated adenocarcinoma, colitis cystica profunda, repair, and other polypoid colitis should not be conflated with adenocarcinoma arising in adenoma—the draft sometimes blurs these entities.
missing_ddx_entities: Endometrioid adenocarcinoma arising in colonic endometriosis (explicitly listed as a DDx in Pathology Outlines).
critic_json.notes_for_revision: Clarify and correct the differential diagnosis table and the distinction between invasive carcinoma, pseudoinvasion, and benign mimics; add missing DDx entity (endometrioid adenocarcinoma arising in endometriosis); sharpen the discussion of 'intramucosal carcinoma' as pTis (not invasive in colon); and explicitly discuss the role of immunostains for tumor origin. Add explicit morphologic grading statistics if possible. Avoid blending features of related but different polypoid lesions and cancers.
